endorsements.quote: Therefore, the research team has proposed a six-month prospective and non-interventional ‘silent trial’ whereby SERP and PACS would run alongside one another, but the SERP score would remain unknown to the triage nurse and not be used in practise.
Even if SERP is successful over time, EDs should constantly monitor effectiveness and safety.

The risk scale would remain 1–4 which would create minimal disruptions to workflow, and the triage nurse would still be at liberty to use his/her clinical judgement to override the score based on clinical experience and expertise.

unlisted_practices: Evaluate AI triage tools in real-world clinical practice through ongoing evaluation-type or hybrid implementation studies rather than relying solely on retrospective accuracy or a head-to-head RCT where an RCT is infeasible.
Establish a baseline performance level that the AI tool must surpass to be considered valuable, and evaluate against it.
Use retrospective comparative studies of AI implementation versus standard triage alone to check for increased rates of untraceable false positives from self-fulfilling predictions.
Prefer inherently interpretable models over post-hoc explanations of black-box models for clinical AI.
Align the AI risk threshold with local clinical governance requirements and amend it before implementation if guidelines prioritize sensitivity over specificity.
Frame the AI tool as decision support that informs rather than dictates care pathways, with final decisions by clinicians.
Collect data on how technology bias and automation bias affect real-world AI performance during evaluation.

screen.reason: This is a bioethics and governance case study/commentary discussing the ethical appropriateness of implementation strategies (e.g., ongoing evaluation within a learning health system framework vs. RCT) for an ED risk prediction tool.
